title: Sessions, JWT & Refresh Tokens
objectives: Weigh server-side sessions against stateless JWTs honestly
Design refresh token rotation with reuse detection
Choose token storage with the XSS tradeoff made explicit
Plan expiry and revocation before tokens exist, not after an incident
body:
Two families of tokens dominate web auth. Server sessions keep state: the cookie holds an opaque id, the server looks up everything else — trivially revocable, at the cost of a shared store. JWTs carry signed claims: any service can verify them without a lookup — fast and stateless, at the cost of revocation. Neither is universally right; the honest choice depends on whether you need instant invalidation.

## The problem
Your team picked JWTs because 'stateless scales', and now a leaked token cannot be invalidated before its 24-hour expiry. Meanwhile a sister team stores tokens in localStorage and wonders what an XSS bug implies. Both are token-design questions that must be answered before launch.

## Constraints
- A JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone holding it can read its claims.
- Stateless verification means no central kill switch — revocation needs state (a denylist) and stops being stateless.
- localStorage is readable by any script on the page; an HttpOnly cookie is not readable by scripts but is exposed to CSRF (mitigated by SameSite + tokens).
- Long-lived access tokens widen the window of every theft; short ones need refresh machinery.

## Options
```json
{
  "access_token": {
    "header": { "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT" },
    "payload": { "sub": "user-42", "scope": "invoices:read", "exp": 1787000000 },
    "lifetime": "5-15 minutes",
    "notes": "short-lived; presented on every request"
  },
  "refresh_token": {
    "storage": "server-side, hashed, one per session",
    "lifetime": "days-weeks",
    "rotation": "every use: old token dies, new one issued",
    "reuse_detection": "presenting an already-rotated token = theft signal; kill the whole session"
  },
  "transport": {
    "preferred": "HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax cookie",
    "localStorage": "XSS becomes session hijack — acceptable only when constraints force it"
  }
}
```

Refresh rotation with reuse detection gives you most of JWT's statelessness with a recovery path: the server only stores hashed refresh tokens, and a replayed old refresh token reveals theft and burns the session.

## Tradeoffs
Server sessions need a shared store (Redis) and a lookup per request; JWTs move that cost to token size on every request and to header parsing. Rotation adds a write per refresh and client logic to handle 401-then-refresh flows. Cookies invite CSRF defenses (previous module); localStorage invites XSS consequences — the storage choice is choosing which attack class you engineer against.

## Decision
Default to server-side sessions in an HttpOnly cookie for traditional apps — revocation stays one DELETE. Choose short-lived JWTs with rotating refresh tokens when multiple services must verify identity independently. In both cases: minutes-long access tokens, hashed refresh tokens server-side, reuse detection, and no tokens in localStorage unless the architecture truly forces it.

## Measure it
Verify what you shipped: assert Set-Cookie attributes in integration tests; time token verification and session lookups under load if you chose sessions; rehearse revocation — log out, change password, and confirm every old access token fails within seconds. Track mean token lifetime and the count of reuse-detection triggers; a trigger that does not kill the session is a bug.

## Best practices
- Keep access tokens short-lived; do the heavy lifting with rotating refresh tokens.
- Store refresh tokens server-side, hashed, and detect reuse to kill compromised sessions.
- Prefer HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookies over localStorage for token transport.
- Include only necessary claims; tokens are read by anyone who holds them.
- Define logout as server-side invalidation, not client-side token deletion.

## Common mistakes
- Issuing 30-day JWTs and calling logout a UI state change.
- Putting sensitive data in JWT payloads and forgetting signatures are not encryption.
- Storing refresh tokens in localStorage, converting any XSS into permanent account takeover.
- Verifying JWTs without checking algorithm and expiry (alg none, missing exp).
- Designing revocation after the first leaked token instead of before launch.

## Production considerations
- Key rotation: sign tokens with versioned keys so compromise of one key invalidates only its era.
- Reuse detection must alert AND terminate the session; log the session id and user for the investigation.
- Size discipline: JWTs ride every request header — bloat shows up as CDN and proxy limits, not just bytes.
- When migrating between session and JWT models, support both verification paths during the transition window and test them separately.

exercise.prompt: Build a token storage advisor. For each app context, recommend where to put tokens and the key consequence: has-xss-history → HttpOnly cookie (scripts cannot read it); needs-instant-revoke → server session (delete one row); multi-service-verification → short JWT + rotating refresh (stateless verification); api-for-mobile → short JWT + secure storage (no browser cookie jar). Implement the advisor.
hints: Each context maps to one storage/model choice plus its consequence — pair them.
instant-revoke is the classic argument for server sessions over stateless JWTs.
multi-service is the classic argument for short JWTs with rotation.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental revocation problem with stateless JWTs?
options: Any service can verify a token without a lookup, so there is no central state that can invalidate it
JWTs cannot carry an expiry claim
Refresh tokens cannot be revoked at all
questions.explanation: Statelessness is the feature that creates the problem: verification requires no shared state, so a token stays valid until its exp no matter what happened to the account.

questions.prompt: Why is localStorage a risky place for session tokens?
options: Browsers clear it on every restart
Any script running on the page can read it, so one XSS bug becomes session theft
It cannot store strings longer than 64 characters
It is only available on mobile browsers
questions.explanation: localStorage has no isolation from page scripts; HttpOnly cookies were invented precisely to keep tokens out of script reach.
